title: Ice Ages

paragraphs.text: The Earth has experienced several ice ages – cold periods marked by glaciers and ice sheet cover. However, the term 'Ice Age' has come to denote the last of these, which began about 70,000 years ago and ended 10,000 years ago.

The concept of ice ages is fairly new. Although people in the early 18th century were aware of the evidence that would eventually be used to prove the existence of the Ice Age, such as large boulders that didn’t seem to belong, mounds of rock debris, and scratches and grooves on the sides of mountains, they attributed this evidence to a giant flood.

Then, in 1785, the Scottish geologist James Hutton presented a theory based on observations of rock formations made during his extensive geographical tours of Britain and Europe. He proposed that the Earth was much older than had previously been believed, and that its surface was continually being recycled and regenerated.

The idea of the Ice Age came from Switzerland, where geological clues led some to believe that the alpine glaciers existing there must once have been more extensive. In 1837, Louis Agassiz, a naturalist fascinated by these signs, presented this idea to a group of scientists, who were underwhelmed by his hypothesis. Regardless of their disbelief, Agassiz was determined to show how glaciers had affected the world. By measuring the long, narrow grooves cut deep into the sides of mountains and observing the layers in the rocks to measure how thick the glaciers and ice sheets must have been, Agassiz and other scientists established that thousands of years ago there had been glaciers and ice sheets a mile deep over parts of northern Europe.

It is now known that in the Ice Age about one third of the world, mostly in the northern hemisphere, was under thick ice. In what is now North America, ice covered Canada and much of the central United States. In Europe, ice covered Scandinavia, Ireland, Germany and western Russia. It took thousands of years to form these massive ice sheets, with layers of snow piling up into thick masses of ice, growing thicker and denser as the weight of new snow and ice layers compressed the old ones. Since the water creating the snow and ice originated from the oceans, their levels consequently dropped 350 to 400 feet.

The glaciers weren’t static. In fact, they’ve often been described as bulldozers, advancing and receding, and leaving behind piles of rocks and other natural debris. And even though the ice wasn’t everywhere, its environmental impact spread far and wide. The outskirts of the glaciers turned into arctic deserts, and the grinding motion of the moving glaciers created a thick kind of dust which was blown across the land.

The glaciers also preserved the fossils of plants and animals which lived through this chilly time. The global temperatures during the Ice Age were about 10 degrees Fahrenheit lower than they are today. It may not sound like much, but when we look at the adaptations that animals of the time made, we know it must have had an impact. They adapted to the cold temperatures by building up reserves of fat and growing specialized coats. The ancestor of the musk ox, for example, developed shaggy hair two feet long and underwool, features that its descendant retains. These served as insulation and were more effective than other animal fur.

There are many theories about why ice ages occur. However, despite what many people think, ice ages do not necessarily occur when the world gets very cold. It’s more the case that it doesn’t get warm enough in the summer. In the 1920s, a scientist named Milutin Milanković worked out why summers may become cooler by looking at the factors that limit how much sunlight our planet receives, the tilt of the Earth’s axis, the closeness of the Earth to the Sun, and how the Earth wobbles on its axis. By examining these factors, and by using a mathematical formula, he was able to calculate the frequency with which ice ages would occur in the future. Today, his calculations are generally accepted by the scientific community.

The movement of the plates on the outer layer of the Earth, known as plate tectonics, also appears to play a role. Over millions of years, plate tectonics can result in the movement of entire continents, with landmasses moving away from warm tropical latitudes towards more northern and southern ones. Then glaciers are more likely to form as a result of the cooler temperatures. They also become more probable when collisions occur between the Earth’s plates, since this may lead to the formation of mountain ranges with higher altitudes.

More recently, studies of trapped air from glacial ages have indicated that there was relatively little carbon dioxide and other gases in the atmosphere during these periods. When these gases are abundant, they trap energy and keep it close to Earth, thus keeping the planet warm. When they become scarcer, that radiant energy escapes. Scientists don’t know exactly why these gases decreased, but this does seem to have contributed to the drop in temperatures that occurred at these times
